action_criteria.expected_evidence: Ceftriaxone given with monitoring (non-severe penicillin rash, low cross-reactivity); stop metformin (lactate 4.8 mmol/L, creatinine 2.1 mg/dL); hold propranolol, lisinopril and diuretics; avoid sedatives
action_criteria.label: Medication review: ceftriaxone with the penicillin allergy (rash), metformin with lactate 4.8 and kidney injury, and propranolol, lisinopril and diuretics in hemorrhagic shock
action_criteria.rationale: The penicillin allergy bears on the mandatory ceftriaxone, and metformin, lisinopril, propranolol and diuretics are unsafe in shock with kidney injury and a raised lactate [Baveno_VII]

prohibited_recommendations: Do not give scheduled or long-acting benzodiazepines; treat alcohol withdrawal symptom-triggered with the lowest effective dose of lorazepam or oxazepam and close monitoring of consciousness (EASL ALD 2018).
Do not prescribe sedating opioids, which worsen hepatic encephalopathy; use acetaminophen up to 2 g per day for pain.
Do not continue metformin: lactate 4.8 mmol/L with kidney injury in decompensated cirrhosis.
Do not transfuse to a normal hemoglobin: liberal transfusion raises portal pressure and rebleeding (Baveno VII).
Do not withhold ceftriaxone because of the penicillin rash.
required_recommendations: Variceal bleeding: vasoactive drug now, ceftriaxone 1 g daily for up to 7 days, restrictive transfusion to hemoglobin 7-8 g/dL, upper endoscopy within 12 hours after resuscitation (Baveno VII); the penicillin allergy (rash) is not a contraindication: cross-reactivity with ceftriaxone is low; give with monitoring.
Protect the airway: grade III HE (GCS 10) with an active upper GI bleed; intubate for airway protection before endoscopy (Baveno VII).
Blood, urine and ascitic cultures are drawn before the first antibiotic dose, which is not delayed for them.

Stop metformin (lactate 4.8 mmol/L, creatinine 2.1 mg/dL) and use insulin for glucose control; hold propranolol, lisinopril, spironolactone and furosemide during the bleed with hypotension and kidney injury (Baveno VII; EASL 2018).
Replace potassium to 4.0 mEq/L or more and magnesium (1.4 mg/dL), because hypokalemia increases renal ammoniagenesis; raise the sodium (129 mEq/L) by no more than 8 mEq/L in 24 hours.

Lactulose by retention enema (300 mL in 700 mL water) every 4-6 hours until oral or nasogastric dosing is safe, then 25 mL every 1-2 hours until at least two soft bowel movements, titrated to 2-3 soft bowel movements per day (ACG 2026 recommendation 10; EASL 2022); avoid over-titration, which causes dehydration, hypokalemia and kidney injury. Continue rifaximin 550 mg twice daily by nasogastric tube.

Refer for liver transplant assessment once stable: decompensated cirrhosis with recurrent overt HE, MELD-Na 37 (EASL 2018); offer treatment for alcohol use disorder, since continued drinking precludes listing.

avoided_actions.rationale: Amyloid PET has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the issue, not Alzheimer pathology.
DaTscan has no role in HE workup; the question is metabolic encephalopathy, not nigrostriatal degeneration.

accepted: Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade III), alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C, MELD-Na 37), precipitated by acute variceal hemorrhage with melena; metformin on the medication list is a separate concern (lactate 4.8 mmol/L with kidney injury).

differential.key_features: Leucocytosis in a bleeding cirrhotic with ascites; the ascitic PMN of 186 cells/mm3 (below 250), a clean urine and sterile blood cultures exclude SBP and another infective source.
Creatinine 2.1 mg/dL with BUN 78 in hemorrhagic shock is pre-renal kidney injury; HRS-AKI cannot be diagnosed while shock persists; reassess after volume, albumin and control of bleeding.
Coagulopathy (INR 3.1, platelets 54) raises the risk; no focal deficit, and the CT shows no hemorrhage.
Daily heavy drinking; no ophthalmoplegia or nystagmus; thiamine is given empirically before any glucose.

key_clinical_evidence: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grade, evidence of liver disease and exclusion of other causes of altered mental status (ACG 2026; EASL 2022).

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleed, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia/hyponatremia), constipation, sedative/CNS-depressant use, dehydration, dietary protein load, renal failure.
Bleeding cirrhotics should receive empiric ceftriaxone prophylaxis (any source) — proven to reduce 30-day mortality.
Variceal hemorrhage is among the top HE precipitants given the nitrogen load.
Child-Pugh C (15: bilirubin 14.8 3, albumin 1.9 3, INR 3.1 3, moderate ascites 3, HE grade 3 3); MELD-Na 37 (creatinine 2.1, bilirubin 14.8, INR 3.1, sodium 129)

An elevated ammonia neither grades nor confirms hepatic encephalopathy and repeat levels are not used to guide treatment; a normal ammonia in a confused patient with cirrhosis should prompt a search for another cause (ACG 2026 recommendation 5 and key concept 14; EASL 2022).
A non-severe penicillin rash does not contraindicate ceftriaxone: cross-reactivity with third-generation cephalosporins is low, so the prophylaxis is given with monitoring.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. R. is a 61-year-old Hispanic man with severe alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C, MELD-Na 26 at his last clinic review) and prior grade III esophageal varices who was brought to the emergency department by his wife for progressive confusion and black tarry stools over the past 24 hours. The wife reports he was increasingly confused yesterday afternoon, could not recognize their grandchildren at dinner, and by this morning could not state his own name. She found bloody-appearing black stool in the toilet bowl multiple times. He has been drinking alcohol daily despite medical advice — wife confirms he drank yesterday. On arrival he is hemodynamically compromised with blood pressure 98/58, heart rate 122, and pale conjunctiva. His wife explains that he has been on lactulose and rifaximin for secondary HE prophylaxis following an episode 8 months ago. His rectal exam reveals melena. He also takes metformin for type 2 diabetes.

neurological_exam.additional: Icteric sclera. Jaundice. Firm, nodular liver edge palpable 3 cm below right costal margin. Moderate ascites with shifting dullness. Multiple spider angiomata on chest. Palmar erythema. Fetor hepaticus present. Melena on rectal exam — active GI bleed confirmed.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 3 mm bilaterally, reactive. Gaze intact. Facial symmetry preserved. No nystagmus.
neurological_exam.mental_status: GCS 10 (E2V3M5). Severely disoriented — does not know name, date, or location. Slow, slurred speech. Asterixis: prominent bilateral flapping tremor at wrists and metacarpophalangeal joints.
neurological_exam.motor: Moves all four limbs. No focal paresis. Increased tone bilateral arms and legs.
neurological_exam.reflexes: DTRs 2+ throughout. Bilateral plantar responses equivocal.
